triples.source_text: Hear this word of the Lord that I take up over you as a lament, house of Israel:

target_units.text: “And you, take up a lament over Israel’s ruler,

triples.relationship: prophetic lament taken up over Israel
triples.rationale: Amos introduces the word taken up over Israel's house as a lament. Ezekiel likewise receives a command to take up a lament over Israel's ruler. Both explicitly frame the prophetic address as lament, with different stated subjects.

triples.source_text: “Virgin Israel has fallen; she will certainly not rise again. She stumbled upon her land; no one will raise her.”

target_units.text: And you will say this word to them: Bring tears down upon your eyes day and night, and let them not cease, because the daughter of My people was utterly crushed, with a very painful wound.
If I go out to the plain, behold, those wounded by the sword; and if I enter the city, behold, the pain of famine! For priest and prophet went to a land they did not know.

triples.relationship: the people pictured as a devastated daughter
triples.rationale: Amos laments fallen Virgin Israel, who has no one to raise her. Jeremiah calls for continuing tears over the crushed daughter of the people and describes sword and famine. Both use a female figure for the people within a lament over national devastation.

triples.source_text: For thus says the Lord, the Lord: “From the city out of which a thousand went, a hundred will remain, and from the one out of which a hundred went, ten will remain for Israel’s house.”

target_units.text: And you shall be left few in number, whereas you were as the stars of heaven in multitude, because you did not hearken unto the voice of the Lord your God.

triples.relationship: a greatly reduced remnant of Israel
triples.rationale: Amos predicts that only a hundred will remain from a city where a thousand went out, and ten from a hundred. Deuteronomy likewise warns that the people will be left few in number after their former multitude, linking their reduction to disobedience.

triples.source_text: For thus says the Lord to Israel’s house: “Seek Me and you will live!

target_units.text: Listen with your ears, and follow My ways; listen to Me, and your soul will live amid good things. And I will make with you an everlasting covenant: the holy and sure blessings of David.
Behold, I have given him as a testimony among the nations, a ruler and commander of nations.
Nations that did not know you will call upon you, and peoples that do not know you will flee to you for refuge, because of your God, the Holy One of Israel, for He has glorified you.
Seek God, and when you find Him, call upon Him; and when He draws near to you,

triples.relationship: seeking and hearing God associated with life
triples.rationale: Amos commands Israel to seek the Lord and live. Isaiah likewise calls for listening to God so that the soul will live and then commands seeking God. Both connect turning toward God with life.

triples.source_text: Do not seek Bethel, do not enter Gilgal, and do not cross over to the Well of the Oath; for Gilgal will certainly be taken captive, and Bethel will be as though it did not exist.”

target_units.text: But you, Israel, do not be ignorant; and Judah, do not enter Gilgal or go up to the house of On, and do not swear by the living Lord.

triples.rationale: Amos tells the people not to enter Gilgal while rejecting their resort to named sanctuaries. Hosea likewise explicitly tells Judah not to enter Gilgal. The connection rests on the identical place and prohibition, without equating the passages' other place names.

triples.source_text: Seek the Lord and live, so that Joseph’s house does not flare up like fire; it will devour him, and there will be no one to quench it for Israel’s house.

target_units.text: House of David, thus says the Lord: Judge a judgment in the morning, set things straight, and rescue the plundered from the hand of the one wronging him, so that My anger is not kindled like fire and burns with no one to quench it.

triples.relationship: warning of fire with no one to quench it
triples.rationale: Amos calls for seeking the Lord so that Joseph's house does not flare up in an unquenchable fire. Jeremiah likewise calls David's house to just action so that the Lord's anger is not kindled like fire with no one to quench it. The warnings address different houses.

triples.source_text: The Lord makes judgment on high and has placed righteousness upon the earth,

target_units.text: Cloud and gloom surround Him; righteousness and judgment are the establishment of His throne.

triples.relationship: the Lord's rule described through righteousness and judgment
triples.rationale: Amos positively describes the Lord making judgment on high and placing righteousness upon the earth. The psalm likewise names righteousness and judgment as the establishment of His throne. This connection preserves Amos's positive native wording.

triples.source_text: making all things and refashioning them, turning death’s shadow into morning and darkening day into night; He calls for the sea’s water and pours it upon the earth’s surface. The Lord God Almighty is His name,

target_units.text: He builds His ascent into heaven and establishes His promise upon the earth; He calls for the sea’s water and pours it upon the earth’s surface. The Lord God Almighty is His name.

triples.relationship: same-book repeated description of the Lord's power over waters
triples.rationale: Both passages describe the Lord calling for the sea's water and pouring it upon the earth's surface, then name Him the Lord God Almighty. The repeated description connects the book's presentations of His power.

triples.source_text: the One distributing shattering against strength and bringing suffering upon a fortress.

target_units.text: and he will bring low the height of your wall’s refuge, and it will descend to the ground.

triples.rationale: Amos describes shattering directed against strength and suffering brought upon a fortress. Isaiah likewise announces the height of a wall's refuge being brought low to the ground, sharing the overthrow of fortified strength.

triples.source_text: They hated one who reproved at the gates and abhorred a holy word.

target_units.text: One who disciplines evil people will receive dishonor for himself, and one who reproves an impious person will bring blame on himself.
Do not reprove evil people, so that they may not hate you; reprove a wise person, and he will love you.

triples.relationship: hatred directed at one who reproves wrongdoing
triples.rationale: Amos accuses the people of hating one who reproves at the gates. Proverbs likewise warns that reproving evil people brings dishonor and hatred, describing the hostile reception of correction.

triples.source_text: Therefore, because you struck the poor with fists and accepted choice gifts from them, you built houses of polished stone but certainly will not inhabit them; you planted desirable vineyards but certainly will not drink their wine.

target_units.text: You shall take a wife, and another man shall have her; you shall build a house, and shall not dwell therein; you shall plant a vineyard, and shall not gather its fruit.

triples.relationship: houses and vineyards whose benefits are lost
triples.rationale: Amos warns those who exploit the poor that they will not inhabit their stone houses or drink their vineyards' wine. Deuteronomy's curse likewise describes a house built but not inhabited and a vineyard planted without gathering its fruit.

triples.source_text: For I knew your many impieties, and your sins are strong: trampling the righteous, taking payments and turning aside the poor at the gates.

target_units.text: You shall not pervert the judgment of a poor man in his cause.
You shall keep far away from every unrighteous charge; the innocent and the righteous you shall not kill, neither shall you justify the ungodly for gifts.
And you shall receive no gifts; for gifts blind the eyes of those who see, and corrupt righteous words.

triples.relationship: payments and injustice toward the poor and righteous
triples.rationale: Amos condemns trampling the righteous, taking payments and turning the poor aside at the gates. Exodus forbids perverting a poor person's judgment, killing the innocent or righteous, and accepting gifts that corrupt righteous words.

triples.source_text: Seek the good and not the evil, so that you may live; then the Lord God Almighty will be with you, just as you said,

target_units.text: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor what is evil; cling to what is good.

triples.relationship: the ethical contrast of good and evil
triples.rationale: Amos commands seeking good rather than evil. Romans likewise commands abhorring evil and clinging to good, presenting the same opposed directions of conduct.

triples.source_text: “We have hated evil things and loved good things.” Restore judgment at the gates, so that the Lord God Almighty may have mercy on Joseph’s remaining ones.

target_units.text: You shall appoint judges and recording officers for yourself in all your cities which the Lord your God gives you, according to your tribes; and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment.
They shall not pervert judgment, neither shall they show partiality, nor take a bribe; for bribes blind the eyes of the wise, and overthrow the words of the righteous.
You shall pursue justly that which is just, that you may live, and enter and inherit the land which the Lord your God gives you.

triples.relationship: restoration of just judgment in the community
triples.rationale: Amos commands restoring judgment at the gates so that the Lord may have mercy on Joseph's remaining ones. Deuteronomy requires appointed judges to judge righteously in the cities, forbids perverted judgment and commands pursuit of justice. The link concerns the required public administration of justice.

triples.source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord God Almighty: “In every square there will be mourning, and in every road it will be said, ‘Alas, alas!’ A farmer will be called to mourning and lamentation and to those skilled in wailing,

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Call the women who lament, and let them come; send for the skilled women, and let them speak,
and let them take up a dirge over you; let your eyes bring down tears, and let your eyelids flow with water.
For a voice of lament was heard in Zion: How we suffered misery and were greatly ashamed, because we abandoned the land and threw away our dwellings!
Hear God’s word now, women, and let your ears receive His mouth’s words; teach your daughters lament, and each woman her neighbor a dirge.

triples.relationship: summoning skilled mourners for a public lament
triples.rationale: Amos announces mourning in squares and roads and a call involving those skilled in wailing. Jeremiah likewise summons skilled women who lament to take up a dirge and teach lamentation. Both explicitly describe organized public mourning.

triples.source_text: and in every road there will be mourning, because I will pass through your midst,” said the Lord.

target_units.text: I will go through the land of Egypt that night and strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both human and animal. Against all the Egyptians’ gods I will execute vengeance. I am the Lord.

triples.relationship: the Lord passing through a people in judgment
triples.rationale: Amos announces mourning because the Lord will pass through the people's midst. Exodus likewise announces His passage through Egypt to strike the firstborn and execute vengeance. The shared passage-and-judgment pattern is applied to different peoples.

triples.source_text: Woe to those desiring the Lord’s day! Why is this Lord’s day for you? It is darkness, not light,

target_units.text: Blow a trumpet in Zion! Proclaim on My holy mountain, and let all who inhabit the land be thrown into turmoil, because the Lord’s day is present; it is near,

a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist. Like dawn a numerous and strong people will be poured over the mountains. Its like has never existed, nor will another follow it through the years, for generations upon generations.

triples.relationship: the Lord's day described as darkness
triples.rationale: Amos warns those who desire the Lord's day that it is darkness rather than light. Joel likewise describes the near Lord's day as darkness and gloom, with turmoil among the land's inhabitants.

triples.source_text: as when someone flees from a lion and a bear falls upon him, then leaps into his house, braces his hands upon the wall, and a snake bites him.

target_units.text: Fear, pit and trap are upon you who dwell on the earth!
Whoever flees the fear will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs from the pit will be caught by the trap, because windows from heaven have opened and the earth’s foundations will be shaken.

triples.relationship: escape from one danger leads into another
triples.rationale: Amos depicts fleeing a lion only to meet a bear, followed by a snake within a house. Isaiah similarly depicts fleeing fear into a pit and climbing from the pit only to be caught by a trap. Both use successive dangers to expose the failure of attempted escape.
